canonical_topic: Up-front premium cost determines whether an option (or lottery ticket) is a good investment
definition: A favorable payoff shape (small risk, large potential reward) does not by itself make an option a good investment. What matters is the price paid to enter: a free or cheap option can be a great investment, but an option purchased for too high a premium becomes a guaranteed-loss position regardless of how attractive its payoff structure looks.
core_idea: Attractive asymmetric payoffs are not sufficient to judge an investment — the entry cost has to be weighed against the expected value, or a high-priced option becomes what the author calls a 'risk-free way to lose money.'
key_points: A free lottery ticket / option would be a great investment by definition.
High up-front costs can turn even a favorable-looking payoff structure into a poor investment.
The author's phrase: overpriced lottery tickets and options can become 'risk-free ways to lose money.'
relationships: Complements the extrinsic value formula — paying more than expected value less intrinsic value erodes the trade's edge
trading_implications: Evaluating an option purchase requires comparing the premium against the option's calculated expected/extrinsic value, not just judging the shape of the payoff.
caveats: The author explicitly warns against the misconception that low risk plus high potential payoff automatically means a good investment — price paid is the deciding factor.
